newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portuguese skinheads jailed for racist killing.
newsitem.headline: Portuguese skinheads jailed for racist killing.

text.p: A judge sentenced 11 skinheads to between 14 and 18 years in jail on Wednesday for beating to death a young black man in a racially-motivated killing which provoked outrage in Portugal.
They were among a group of 50 skinheads who rampaged through Lisbon in the early hours one weekend in June 1995, attacking blacks with iron rods and baseball bats.

At least 12 people of African origin were injured in the attacks in the Bairro Alto suburb, a popular tourist haunt, and Alcindo Monteiro, a 27-year-old Portuguese citizen of Cape Verdean origin, later died of injuries to his brain and spine.

The state prosecutor's office had sought sentences for murder ranging from 12 to 20 years for 11 of the 17 accused after a four-month trial, court officials said. Portugal does not have a death penalty for murder.
All the accused were acquitted of a charge of genocide, but, as well as the 11 sentenced for murder, four were jailed for two to four years for grievous bodily harm and two were found innocent.
Defence lawyer Joao Nabais said he did not believe that the skinheads had intended to systematically wipe out every black person who crossed their path on the night of the murder.

Relatives and some anti-racist campaigners said the sentences were a fair punishment for the crime. "I think justice was done. This is good news for the fight against racism," Manuel Correia, president of the Anti-Racist Front, said.
Monteiro's father and sister said they thought the sentences were fair. "I think justice was done," his sister told Channel One television.
But one prominent anti-racist activist, Jose Falcao of SOS Racismo, said the skinheads should have been found guilty of genocide. He said most of those who ran amok in Lisbon had escaped unpunished.
"They should have been found guilty of genocide because this is a gang, a political organisation of the extreme right that kills," Falcao told TSF radio.
After the verdict, dozens of skinheads and relatives of the defendants threatened journalists whom they blamed for publicity that led to the sentences. Many relatives wept hysterically.
The judge had accepted a request by defence lawyers to ban photographers and cameramen from broadcasting images of the trial in order to avoid sensational publicity.
The killing of Monteiro shocked Portugal to the core and President Mario Soares appealed for calm among Africans in the country.
Portugal has long become accustomed to racial tolerance after the assimilation of blacks from former colonies in Africa into Portuguese society.

Monteiro could be a symbol of Portugal's tradition of racial integration. Born in the Cape Verde islands off West Africa, he spent his last 16 years working in an office in Portugal, had a record of good conduct and carried a Portuguese national identity card, colleagues and relatives said.
Parliament held a minute's silence in his memory days after the attack, condemned by politicians across party lines.
Portugal, with a population of 10 million, has some 170,000 registered foreign residents.
The government estimates there may be up to 70,000 illegal immigrants, many from former colonies, but unofficial estimates range up to 150,000 illegal immigrants.

The last major racist incident in Portugal took place in October 1989 when skinheads attacked supporters of the extreme left-wing Socialist Revolutionary Party and stabbed one of its leaders to death.
